author: Clement of Alexandria
occasion: A fragment of moral and spiritual instruction addressed to a recent convert, guiding the new believer in conduct, speech, self-control, and trust in God.
argument: The author urges the newly baptized to cultivate calmness and self-mastery in speech, movement, and emotion, keeping the mind fixed on God so that it rules the passions from a quiet throne. He gives practical rules for measured and modest conversation, respect for others, and avoidance of anger, pride, and mockery. The believer is to direct all words and deeds to God and Christ, turning the soul frequently to God and not letting long sleep hinder prayer and hymns. He is to consider sufficient for the body what is necessary, avoiding meat and wine except when illness requires them for healing, and to choose the joys of divine words and hymns. He should release many cares about the body, trusting that God will provide what is needed, and face sickness and hardship with a strong soul, showing mercy to the afflicted and praying for God's help, looking forward to the eternal blessedness the Son of God will bring.

outline.move: Cultivate calm in words, deeds, speech, and walk; avoid rash vehemence so the mind remains steady and rules the passions from a quiet throne, and avoid signs of pride.
Speak gently and with forethought, listen in turn, learn gladly, teach generously, honor elders and God's servants, and bear the arrogant with meekness.

Direct all words and deeds to God and Christ, rest the mind in the Savior's divine light, share understanding with people by day but turn to God for the most part at night as well as by day, and do not let much sleep prevail over prayers and hymns to God.

Do not relax the soul through feasting and drink; consider sufficient for the body what is necessary, avoid meat and wine except when illness requires them for healing, and choose the joys of divine words and hymns.

Release many cares about the body, trusting that God will provide necessary food, clothing, and protection from cold, because God owns the whole earth and cares for his servants as his own members and temples.

Face sickness and hardship with a strong and courageous soul, resist pains with an unyielding mind, show mercy to the afflicted, and pray for God's help, looking forward to the eternal blessedness the Son of God will bring.

cast.name: Clement of Alexandria
cast.who: The author, writing moral instruction to a new believer.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Savior, in whom the believer rests and to whom all things are referred.

cast.name: God
cast.who: The Father, to whom the believer directs prayer, hymns, and trust, and who cares for his servants.

cast.name: the Son of God
cast.who: The one who will come at the end to restore good things to his own people.

voices.speaker: Clement of Alexandria
voices.how_marked: The entire text is the author's direct address to the newly baptized, using second-person singular imperatives and exhortations.

key_terms.sense: Calmness, quietness, and self-possession in speech, action, and movement.
Rash vehemence or violent intensity that disturbs the mind and makes it weak.
The mind or intellect, which should rule the passions from a high and quiet throne, looking toward God.
The passions or disordered emotions, such as gluttony, boiling anger, and other impulses that threaten to overpower the mind.
Gluttony or ravenous appetite for food, presented as a passion to be avoided.
Boiling anger or hot temper, one of the passions the mind must control.
Pride or arrogance, shown in haughty posture, lifted head, and affected walk.
Modesty or reverence, especially toward women, expressed in downcast eyes and respectful behavior.
Good speech or graciousness, the manner in which one bears with the proud and insolent.
The soul's tension or firmness, which must not be slackened by feasting and drinking.
Members of God's own body, used of his servants whom he cares for as his own limbs.
Temples, used of believers whom God cares for as his own sacred shrines.
God's commandments, which the believer is to keep with wholehearted purpose.
Eternal blessedness or happiness, which believers will enjoy when the Son of God comes.

scripture: The fragment contains no direct biblical quotations or explicit scriptural citations. If any allusions are identified in translation, follow the Septuagint book names and Psalm numbering customary in Clement's Alexandrian context, and cite them in modern English form (e.g., 'Psalms' with Septuagint numbering noted where it differs from the Hebrew).
uncertain: The exact date of the work is unknown.
The original title of the work is not preserved; 'To the Newly Baptized' is a modern descriptive title for the fragment.
The original length and structure of the work are unknown, since only this fragment survives.
The precise identity of the addressee beyond 'newly baptized' cannot be established from the fragment.
Whether the author was in Alexandria when writing cannot be established from the fragment.
